content:
Ask a sharp student to rank √50 and 7 without a calculator, and watch the pause. That half-second of doubt is where easy marks leak away. Integers, fractions, primes and irrationals all live on one number line, and the Digital SAT loves to test whether you know that neighbourhood cold. This free SAT Math Number System practice test hands you 15 quick MCQs, so you can find the leaks and plug them today.

What the number system covers on the SAT

The exam never labels a question ‘number system’. Instead it hides the topic inside bigger problems. So the basics must be automatic, not effortful. Here is the ground this chapter covers:

  • Integers, whole numbers and natural numbers, and how they nest.
  • Rational numbers, which you can write as a simple fraction.
  • Irrational numbers like √2 and π, which never settle into a neat fraction.
  • Place value, factors, multiples and the divisibility rules.
  • Absolute value and ordering on the number line.

Three habits that raise your SAT Math Number System practice test score

Most students do not need fresh theory. They need faster reflexes. First, memorise the squares up to 15 and the cubes up to 5. Then you spot √144 and √169 on sight. Second, learn the divisibility rules for 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 11 by heart. They turn slow trial-and-error into a two-second check. Third, read absolute value as distance, never as ‘just make it positive’. That framing stops the sign slips that cost careless marks.

Traps the SAT sets, and the quick fix

The exam rarely asks a bare definition. It leans on the gap between a rushed guess and a clean rule. So study the fixes below, because they show up again and again.

Question saysWeak moveStrong move
Is √36 irrational?Assume every root is irrational√36 = 6, so it is rational
Order −3, −7, 2Read −7 as the larger valueOn the line −7 sits left of −3, so it is smaller
Zeros at the end of 20!Count the even numbersCount factors of 5, which gives 4

Why the trailing-zero question fools people

A trailing zero comes from a factor of 10, and 10 is 2 times 5. In a factorial there are always more 2s than 5s. So the count of 5s decides the answer. For 20 factorial you get four multiples of 5, and no extra from 25. Therefore the product ends in exactly four zeros. Slow down here, and the marks are yours.

Why this chapter pays off across the section

Here is the counter-intuitive part. The number system looks like the easiest chapter, yet it quietly powers the hard ones. Ratios rely on clean fraction sense. Exponent questions rest on prime factors. Even the word problems in the calculator module hide a divisibility idea. So strong number sense is not busywork. It is leverage. In my experience coaching SAT students, the ones who drill this chapter early make fewer silly errors everywhere else. And fewer silly errors, not flashy tricks, is what pushes a 650 toward 750.

Rational versus irrational, settled fast

A number is rational when it equals one integer over another. So 0.75 is rational, because it is 3 over 4. A root is rational only when the number under it is a perfect square. Therefore √49 is fine, but √48 is not. Keep that single test ready, and the ‘which of these is irrational’ item becomes a gift.

A quick worked example

Suppose a number leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 5, and a remainder of 3 when divided by 4. Try the small candidates. Numbers that give remainder 2 under 5 are 7, 12, 17, 22 and so on. Now test each against 4. Here 7 leaves 3, so 7 already works. That is the rhythm the SAT rewards: list, test, stop early. You rarely need heavy algebra for these.

quiz.title: SAT Math Number System Quiz
quiz.intro: Fifteen Digital SAT-style questions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: In the numeral 738492, by how much does the place value of the digit 3 exceed its face value?
questions.explanation: The digit 3 sits in the ten-thousands place, so its place value is 30000 and its face value is 3. The required difference is 30000 - 3 = 29997.
Take out the common factor: 12846 x (593 + 407) = 12846 x 1000 = 12846000.

questions.q: The sum of the first 45 natural numbers is
Two numbers are said to be co-prime when their highest common factor (HCF) is
questions.explanation: Co-prime numbers share no common factor other than 1, so their HCF is exactly 1.
Any positive power of a number ending in 5 also ends in 5.

questions.q: If a and b are both odd numbers, which of the following is an even number?
questions.explanation: The sum of two odd numbers is even. The product of two odd numbers is odd, so ab and ab + 2 are odd, and a + b + 1 is odd.

questions.q: The product of two consecutive integers is always
questions.explanation: Of any two consecutive integers one is even, so their product is always even.

questions.q: If the three-digit number 24x is divisible by 3, the possible values of x are
questions.explanation: The digit sum is 2 + 4 + x = 6 + x, which is a multiple of 3 when x is 0, 3, 6 or 9.

questions.q: The largest five-digit number exactly divisible by 99 is
questions.explanation: 99999 / 99 = 1010.09..., and 99 x 1010 = 99990, which is the largest five-digit multiple of 99.

questions.q: When a number is multiplied by 5 and 9 is subtracted from the product, the result is 156. The number is
How many three-digit numbers are there in all?
questions.explanation: Three-digit numbers run from 100 to 999, giving 999 - 100 + 1 = 900.

questions.q: The number of zeros at the end of the product 1 x 2 x 3 x ... x 20 is
questions.explanation: Trailing zeros are determined by factors of 5: floor(20/5) + floor(20/25) = 4 + 0 = 4.
